01 / Look closely

A strange world, an unusual guide.

What strikes you first?

Colourful, eccentric, mysterious.

Present the document.

The document is an image from Alice Through the Looking Glass, a fantasy film directed by James Bobin and released in 2016. It shows Johnny Depp as the Mad Hatter. The image illustrates the opening page of the textbook unit “The Art of Madness”.

Describe the character and his surroundings.

In the foreground, the Mad Hatter is leaning towards us with his arms stretched out. He is smiling and looking directly at the viewer. He has bright orange curly hair, a pale face and colourful make-up around his eyes.

He is wearing an enormous dark top hat with a wide pink ribbon, a large patterned bow tie and a dark red coat. His unusual clothes and exaggerated appearance make him look eccentric and theatrical.

Dark, twisting branches frame the scene. Behind the character, we can see a colourful garden, flowers, large mushrooms and strange buildings in the distance. A grinning cat appears to be floating behind him. These details create a fantasy world in which ordinary rules do not seem to apply.

How do the details create contrasting impressions?

The Mad Hatter’s bright hair, colourful clothes and broad smile suggest playfulness. His direct gaze and open arms may seem to invite us into his world. However, the dark branches and his exaggerated appearance can also make the scene feel unsettling. The picture is both attractive and strange. It encourages us to enter an unfamiliar world and question our usual expectations.

For an interpretation, use “suggests”, “may” or “can”, then support your idea with a visible detail.

02 / Read Wilde

Too important to talk seriously about?

“Life is much too important a thing ever to talk seriously about it.”Oscar Wilde · Lady Windermere’s Fan · quotation reproduced in the textbook

If life is important, how would we normally expect people to talk about it? How does Wilde reverse this expectation?

What we normally expect

Life is important, so we should talk about it seriously.

Wilde’s surprising reasoning

Life is so important that we should never talk seriously about it.

We normally associate importance with seriousness. Wilde reverses this expectation by presenting life’s importance as a reason for avoiding serious talk about it. The paradox lies in this unexpected reasoning. The words “important” and “seriously” are not opposites.

A little help in French

On s’attend à devoir parler sérieusement de la vie parce qu’elle est importante. Wilde renverse ce raisonnement : elle serait trop importante pour qu’on en parle sérieusement. Le paradoxe porte sur le lien établi entre ces deux idées, pas sur une opposition entre deux mots.

La construction too… to… signifie ici « trop… pour… ». Une reformulation naturelle est : « La vie est bien trop importante pour qu’on en parle sérieusement. »

Explain Wilde’s message in your own words.

Wilde’s remark can be read as an invitation to avoid excessive solemnity. Humour and a playful attitude can help us look at life differently. We can value life deeply while making room for laughter, imagination and a lighter way of talking about it. This does not mean that we should ignore our responsibilities.

How does the quotation connect to the picture?

Both documents challenge ordinary expectations. The picture presents an eccentric character in an imaginative world. Wilde’s remark challenges the belief that important things must always be discussed seriously. Both invite us to look beyond what seems normal or obvious.

03 / Follow the logic

A very official announcement.

“To stop students being late, we will remove all the clocks. Without an official time, nobody can officially be late.”

Identify the problem, the proposed solution and its limit.

Part of the argumentExplanation
The real problemStudents arrive late.
The absurd solutionRemove all the clocks.
Its internal logicWithout an official time, nobody can officially be recorded as late.
Its limitStudents can still arrive after the lesson has started. The rule changes how lateness is recorded instead of preventing it.

Nonsense with an internal logic

The steps of a strange argument connect, even though its conclusion is absurd or impractical. Here, the Ministry treats the measurement of lateness as if it were the cause of lateness. Its rule hides the problem instead of solving it.

Deadpan humour

Deadpan humour means delivering something funny or absurd with a serious face and a calm voice. The contrast between the absurd content and the serious delivery creates humour.

En français : deadpan humour = humour pince-sans-rire. Le flegme désigne plutôt le calme imperturbable d’une personne.

04 / Take the floor

Our first rule as Ministers.

Present one absurd rule that targets a real problem. Explain your reasoning with a perfectly serious delivery.

One possible announcement

“Ladies and gentlemen, welcome to the Ministry of Nonsense. Too much paper is wasted at school. From now on, all tests must be imaginary. Students will answer in their heads, so we will never need to print anything. As a result, we will save paper. Thank you for supporting this excellent reform.”

Why is the solution absurd?

Imaginary tests would save paper, but the teacher would be unable to check the students’ answers. The solution defeats one of the purposes of a test. It follows a kind of logic, but it creates a new problem.

Useful sentence starters

  • Identify a problem: We want to stop… / We want to reduce…
  • Announce a rule: From now on, everyone must… / Nobody is allowed to…
  • Explain a result: This will… because… / As a result,…
05 / Keep an idea

The essential lesson.

The picture shows the Mad Hatter, an eccentric character in a colourful but unsettling fantasy world. His unusual appearance challenges ordinary expectations. Wilde’s quotation also reverses an expectation: he presents life’s importance as a reason for avoiding serious talk about it. Humour can help us look at familiar things differently. Nonsense can follow its own internal logic, even when its conclusion is absurd. With deadpan humour, an absurd idea is delivered with a calm voice and a serious face. It can make us laugh and think.

Our big question: How does British art turn madness into a creative power?

Today: one absurd rule to try the technique. Our final mission is now Breaking News from Wonderland: a 2–3 minute news report in groups of three, with a news anchor, a reporter and a witness.

Lesson 02 · Long Live the Fools!

Licensed to Laugh.
Allowed to Question?

01 / Observe

The king and the jester.

Describe one detail for each character. How does the picture bring humour and power together?

The king is seated in rich clothing with a fur-trimmed cloak. The standing jester wears a colourful red, green and yellow costume and leans towards him with a small figure on a stick. The contrast between royal dignity and the jester’s playful posture suggests that humour can enter the world of power. The painting alone does not show that the jester has replaced the king.

02 / Read

Festive authority, real limits.

Document A · Skywalks 1ère, p. 94

The Lord of Misrule: The Party Prince of Christmas Past

For hundreds of years, certain communities in Britain and the households of the well-heeled¹ had their own Christmas party coordinator. He was a compère, a ringleader², and an organiser of the feasting and dancing, but was also solemnly ‘crowned’ and given temporary leave to lord it over³ the real lords and nobles before him. [...] This person was the ‘Lord of Misrule’.

The ‘reigns’ of the Lords of Misrule peaked in Britain in the 16th century [...] Henry VIII was a big fan of the office of Lord of Misrule. Henry usually held Christmas at Greenwich Palace, and even foreign visitors commented on the scale and grandeur of the Christmas feasts, which on occasion saw hundreds of guests at the table for seven hours at a time. From Christmas Eve there would be twelve days of banquets, pageants, dancing, and carols, compered by the Lord of Misrule. [Henry] enjoyed the ‘role reversal’ aspect of this tradition, laughing heartily when the Lord of Misrule at his first Christmas as king rudely asked Henry for more money!

Sky History · December 2021 · extract reproduced in the textbook
¹ wealthy people · ² organiser or leader · ³ command

Read the article. Identify two duties of the Lord of Misrule and explain his temporary authority.

He organised feasting, dancing, games and celebrations. He was ceremonially crowned and temporarily allowed to command real lords and nobles. His authority belonged to the Christmas festivities.

Explain “role reversal”. Use the final anecdote, then explain why the king does not actually lose his power.

Role reversal means turning the usual hierarchy upside down. At Henry VIII’s first Christmas as king, the Lord of Misrule rudely asked him for more money, and Henry laughed. A subordinate could address the king unusually freely during the festivities. However, this freedom was temporary and permitted. Henry remained the real monarch.

A key distinction: the Lord of Misrule is a temporary leader of festivities. A court jester has a role at court. These figures share a connection with humour and authority, but the titles are not interchangeable.

03 / Watch

Speaking truth to power.

Who is Will Sommers? · Folger Theatre, 2010 · approximately 1 min 50.

Video provided by Hachette Education · Open on Hachette ↗

First viewing: who was Will Sommers, and what two functions does the actor give to jesters?

Will Sommers was Henry VIII’s court jester. According to the actor, jesters could entertain and speak truth to power: they could draw the monarch’s attention to things that other people would find dangerous to say.

Second viewing: how does the director use Sommers in this production of Henry VIII?

The director adds Sommers as a character even though Shakespeare did not write him into the play. He wants the audience to see events through this clown’s perspective. Sommers is present in every scene, sometimes as a witness, and takes on several roles. He acts as a guide between the story and the audience.

Explain “speak truth to power”. Does the video prove that every jester could say anything without risk?

It means telling people in authority truths they may not want to hear. The actor describes the jester’s special licence to speak more freely than others. This explains the theatrical role of the fool, but it does not prove that every historical jester was always safe from punishment.

Source: Who is Will Sommers? · Folger Theatre, 2010 · video provided by Hachette Education, Skywalks 1ère, p. 94.

04 / Decode and perform

The Fool’s Double Meaning.

Match each apparent compliment to its hidden criticism.

1. Your Majesty, your speeches are excellent. They give us plenty of time to sleep.

Hidden criticism: The king’s speeches are too long and boring.

The first sentence sounds like praise. The second reveals that listeners fall asleep during the speeches.

2. Your Majesty, everyone agrees with you. Nobody dares to speak.

Hidden criticism: People are afraid to disagree with the king.

The apparent agreement comes from fear, not from genuine support.

3. Your Majesty, your taxes work wonders. Our purses have never been lighter.

Hidden criticism: The king’s taxes leave people with too little money.

A lighter purse sounds like a benefit, but it means people have less money because of the taxes.

Explain one double meaning.

“Everyone agrees with you” sounds like a compliment. However, “Nobody dares to speak” shows that people are afraid to disagree. The fool exposes fear at court through an apparently flattering remark.

A possible performance

Fool: Your Majesty, everyone agrees with you. Nobody dares to speak.
King: Thank you. I knew you would appreciate it!
Fool: Of course, Your Majesty.

The king takes the remark as praise. The audience understands the criticism. The fool’s serious delivery adds deadpan humour.

05 / Remember

Humour questions authority.

Exit ticket: how can a fool challenge power without replacing the ruler?

A fool can use humour to expose problems or tell uncomfortable truths. Festive role reversal can also allow temporary freedom. However, permission to joke or criticise is different from holding lasting political power.

The Lord of Misrule temporarily reversed social roles during Christmas festivities. He could command nobles, but the king kept his real power. Will Sommers was Henry VIII’s court jester. In the Folger production, he also guides the audience through the story. Humour can help a fool speak truth to power: it can expose uncomfortable truths. Yet permission to joke is not the same as lasting political authority.

For our news report: an absurd rule should reveal a real problem.

Part 03 · Fools Know Better!

Perfectly Logical.
Completely Absurd.

In class: 5 min recall, 15 min expert pairs (A or B), 12 min exchange, 8 min comparison, 5 min headline. Vocabulary and grammar are completed at home.
01 / Document A

Alice questions the rules.

Read the document as text

“Would you tell me,” said Alice, a little timidly, “why you are painting those roses?”

Five and Seven said nothing, but looked at Two. Two began in a low voice, “Why the fact is, you see, Miss, this here ought to have been a red rose-tree, and we put a white one in by mistake; and if the Queen was to find it out, we should all have our heads cut off, you know. So you see, Miss, we’re doing our best, afore she comes, to—” At this moment Five, who had been anxiously looking across the garden, called out “The Queen! The Queen!” and the three gardeners instantly threw themselves flat upon their faces. [...]

First came ten soldiers carrying clubs, these were all shaped like the three gardeners, oblong and flat, with their hands and feet at the corners: next the ten courtiers; these were ornamented all over with diamonds, and walked two and two, as the soldiers did. After these came the royal children; there were ten of them [...]: they were all ornamented with hearts. Next came the guests, mostly Kings and Queens [...]; and, last of all this grand procession, came THE KING AND QUEEN OF HEARTS.

Alice was rather doubtful whether she ought not to lie down on her face like the three gardeners, but she could not remember ever having heard of such a rule at processions [...].

The Queen said severely “Who is this?” She said it to the Knave of Hearts, who only bowed and smiled in reply.

“Idiot!” said the Queen, tossing her head impatiently; and, turning to Alice, she went on, “What’s your name, child?”

“My name is Alice, so please your Majesty,” said Alice very politely; but she added, to herself, “Why, they’re only a pack of cards, after all. I needn’t be afraid of them!”

“And who are these?” said the Queen, pointing to the three gardeners who were lying round the rose-tree [...].

“How should I know?” said Alice, surprised at her own courage. “It’s no business of mine.”

The Queen [...] screamed “Off with her head! Off—”

“Nonsense!” said Alice, very loudly and decidedly, and the Queen was silent.

Text as reproduced in the textbook. Afore = before · Knave = servant attending the Queen.

A1. Who is afraid of whom? Explain the gardeners’ mistake and their attempted solution.

The gardeners Two, Five and Seven fear the Queen of Hearts. They planted a white rose-tree instead of a red one, so they paint the roses red to hide their mistake. They fear that the Queen will have their heads cut off. The punishment is completely disproportionate.

A2. How does Alice’s attitude change? Support your answer with two adverbs or expressions from the text.

Alice first speaks “a little timidly” and “very politely”. She then realises that the Queen and her court are only playing cards. At the end she says “Nonsense!” “very loudly and decidedly”. She becomes confident and challenges the Queen’s authority.

A3. Find the double meaning of “clubs”. How do the other card suits help organise this strange world?

Clubs means both weapons carried by soldiers and the card suit trèfle. Courtiers wear diamonds, which suggest wealth and status. The royal children wear hearts, like their parents, the King and Queen of Hearts. The gardeners can be associated with spades, both gardening tools and the suit pique, although the extract does not explicitly say that they carry spades. The world is strange but follows a system.

A4. What does this scene criticise? Explain why its nonsense is not simply random.

The scene makes arbitrary, frightening authority look ridiculous. Alice can resist the Queen when she questions her power. The roles of the playing cards also follow a recognisable logic: soldiers have clubs, courtiers diamonds and royal children hearts. Carroll uses absurdity and wordplay to make us question apparently normal rules.

02 / Document B

Brilliant minds, dangerous schemes.

Read the document as text

School of languages

I also went to a school of languages and saw a scheme for completely abolishing all words as a great advantage to people’s health.

The reasoning

The logic was—every word we speak, to some degree, results in the dwindling of our lungs by corrosion, and contributes to the shortening of our lives.

The proposed solution

A solution was suggested that it would be more convenient for all men to carry with them all things necessary to express whatever they were supposed to speak about!

School of political projectors

I was most surprised when I went to the school of political projectors. There, a professor offered a wonderful device to reconcile violent parties.

The proposal

Take a hundred leaders of each party, and divide them into couples—one from each party. Then let two operators saw off the necks of each couple. Then equally divide and interchange the brains, applying each to the head of his opposite-party man.

The promised result

Two half brains being left to debate the matter within the space of one skull would soon come to a good understanding.

Gulliver’s reaction

I saw nothing in this country that could persuade me to stay longer, and I began to think of returning home to England.

Departure

I decided to head to the island of Luggnagg, southeast of Japan, in order to return to Europe.

Reading transcription of the supplied graphic novel page. Panel headings are reading aids. Dwindling = reduction · skull = cranium · rival parties = opposing political groups.

B1. Who is visiting Lagado? Who claims to offer useful knowledge?

Gulliver visits Lagado, a city presented as devoted to learning and progress. He meets scholars and professors at a school of languages and a school of political projectors. Their projects are presented as improvements to health, communication and politics.

B2. For each project, identify the problem, the proposed solution and a likely practical consequence.

Language: the scholars claim speaking damages the lungs and shortens life. They propose abolishing words and carrying the objects people want to discuss. This would make communication difficult and burdensome, especially for abstract ideas. Politics: a professor proposes exchanging halves of rival leaders’ brains to make them agree. Such surgery would be dangerous and could kill them. Agreement is only a promised result in the project, not a demonstrated success.

B3. Why are “solution” and “wonderful device” ironic? Use one example.

These expressions sound positive, but the proposals are impractical or dangerous. For instance, making people carry objects instead of speaking would make communication harder. Calling such an idea a “solution” creates a gap between the confident language and the likely consequences.

B4. What does Gulliver’s final reaction suggest? Is Swift simply saying that all science is bad?

Gulliver finds nothing to persuade him to stay and wants to return to England. His departure expresses rejection of what he has seen. The satire targets intellectual pride, impractical schemes and knowledge disconnected from people’s needs. It does not follow that all science or research is useless.

03 / Compare and report

Breaking News from Wonderland.

Together: explain one similarity and one difference between Carroll’s and Swift’s use of absurdity.

Both make powerful figures or institutions look ridiculous and invite us to question their authority. Carroll focuses on arbitrary rules and the Queen’s frightening behaviour, using a world of playing cards with its own logic. Swift exposes schemes presented as rational progress although they ignore practical consequences.

Newsroom rehearsal: write a headline and a two-sentence introduction about one event in the documents. Reveal the problem behind the official claim.

WHITE ROSES BANNED ACROSS WONDERLAND! The Queen says that only red roses are acceptable. Gardeners are now painting every white flower because a gardening mistake could cost them their lives.

The essential lesson

Carroll and Swift use absurd worlds to question authority. In Wonderland, the Queen’s disproportionate threats expose arbitrary power. Alice gains confidence and challenges it. The playing cards and their roles follow an internal logic based on wordplay. In Lagado, projects presented as rational progress ignore practical consequences. Swift’s irony exposes intellectual pride and impractical schemes. Both writers invite readers to question rules and claims that appear authoritative.

Our final mission

In groups of three, present a 2–3 minute news report from Wonderland. A news anchor announces an absurd decision, a reporter investigates it and a witness explains its consequences. Use a link to the documents studied. The anchor and reporter may keep a serious delivery while the witness reacts. A headline is enough as a visual support. Video editing is not required.

wordplay · Wordplay exploits more than one meaning of a word.

Swift uses humour to criticise scholars and institutions. This is ___.

At home / Grammar

What / Which

Le repère essentiel

WHAT signifie ici « ce que / ce qui ». Il inclut son antécédent : on peut souvent le remplacer par the thing(s) that.

What Alice says surprises the Queen.
Ce qu’Alice dit surprend la Reine.

La proposition What Alice says est le sujet de surprises. Dans Alice questions what the Queen says, la relative est complément de questions.

WHICH reprend un antécédent déjà exprimé. Il peut reprendre un nom non humain, ou une proposition entière.

The scheme which Gulliver describes is absurd.
Which reprend le nom the scheme.

The scholars abolish words, which makes communication harder.
Which reprend le fait de supprimer les mots.

Quand which commente la proposition précédente, on le sépare par une virgule. Ne pas confondre ces emplois relatifs avec what / which dans une question.

Exercises and answers

Alice questions ___ the Queen says.

what · What = the things that. It has no separate antecedent.

The gardeners paint the roses red, ___ surprises Alice.

which · Which refers to the whole preceding event: the gardeners paint the roses red.

___ the professor calls a solution is actually dangerous.

what · The relative clause introduced by what is the subject of is.

The Queen threatens Alice, ___ reveals her arbitrary power.

which · Which comments on the whole preceding clause.

Gulliver rejects a scheme ___ is impractical.

which · Here which refers to the noun phrase a scheme. This is a noun antecedent, not a whole clause.

The reporter explains ___ happened in the garden.

what · What = the thing that / the things that. No separate antecedent comes before it.

“The scholars carry objects, which makes travel difficult.” What does “which” refer to?

The fact that the scholars carry objects. The singular verb makes agrees with a comment on the whole event.

“The scheme which Gulliver describes is absurd.” What is the antecedent of “which”?

The scheme. Which refers to the noun phrase the scheme.

Choose the best explanation of “what” in “What Alice says silences the Queen.”

It means “the thing that Alice says” and introduces the subject of silences. What is a relative word here. The sentence is a statement.

Write a sentence with “what” to explain what the gardeners fear.

What the gardeners fear is the Queen’s punishment. / The gardeners fear what the Queen might do to them. “What” includes the meaning “the thing that” or “the things that”.

At home / Grammar

The scope and position of adverbs

Que précise l’adverbe ?

Un adverbe peut préciser un verbe, un adjectif, un autre adverbe ou l’ensemble d’une proposition. Il faut identifier sa portée : l’élément sur lequel il agit.

ExemplePortée
Alice speaks politely.Politely précise le verbe speaks : comment parle-t-elle ?
The plan is very dangerous.Very intensifie l’adjectif dangerous.
Alice speaks very politely.Very intensifie l’adverbe politely.
Unfortunately, the plan fails.Unfortunately commente la proposition entière.

La place dépend du sens et du type d’adverbe

  • Fréquence : généralement avant le verbe lexical, mais après be. The Queen often threatens people. / Alice is usually polite.
  • Avec un auxiliaire : souvent entre l’auxiliaire et le verbe lexical. They have carefully painted the roses.
  • Manière : souvent après le verbe et son complément. Alice answers the Queen politely. On peut aussi rencontrer Alice politely answers the Queen.
  • Intensité : devant l’adjectif ou l’adverbe modifié. Very dangerous / very politely.

Évite de placer un adverbe de manière entre le verbe et son complément direct : préfère They paint the roses carefully à They paint carefully the roses.

Only : déplacer le mot change la restriction

Only Alice challenges the Queen. → Alice est la seule à la contester.
Alice challenges only the Queen. → Elle ne conteste que la Reine.

Beaucoup d’adverbes se forment avec adjectif + -ly, mais pas tous : often, very, soon sont aussi des adverbes. Certains mots en -ly, comme friendly, sont des adjectifs.

Exercises and answers

Complete with an adverb: Alice replies ___ (polite).

politely · Polite becomes politely. It describes how Alice replies.

Complete with an adverb: the Queen waits ___ (impatient).

impatiently · Impatient becomes impatiently.

Complete with an adverb: Alice speaks ___ (loud).

loudly · Loudly describes how Alice speaks.

Complete with an adverb: the gardeners look around ___ (anxious).

anxiously · Anxious becomes anxiously.

Complete: the plan is very ___ (dangerous / dangerously).

dangerous · After is, dangerous describes the plan. Very modifies the adjective dangerous.

Complete: the professor speaks very ___ (confident / confidently).

confidently · Confidently modifies speaks. Very modifies confidently.

In “Alice speaks very politely”, what does “very” modify?

The adverb politely. Very intensifies politely, which tells us how Alice speaks.

“Only Alice challenges the Queen.” What does “only” focus on?

Alice: nobody else challenges the Queen. Only comes before the focused element Alice.

Which is the usual neutral position of “often”?

The Queen often threatens people. Frequency adverbs usually come before the main lexical verb. They do not normally split a verb from its direct object.

Choose the natural sentence.

The gardeners have carefully painted the roses. Carefully can go between the auxiliary and the past participle. “The gardeners have painted the roses carefully” is also natural.

Write two sentences with “only” in different positions to show two different meanings. Explain them in French.

Only Alice challenges the Queen. = Alice est la seule à la contester. Alice challenges only the Queen. = Elle ne conteste que la Reine, pas les autres personnages. The position of “only” identifies the element being restricted.
